title: What If You Saw Flashes With Your Eyes Shut? Astronauts Do

scenes.text: What if you saw flashes of light with your eyes closed? In space, almost everyone does.
Apollo 11. Armstrong and Aldrin both reported it: spots, streaks, little clouds of white light, blindfolded or not.
In the dark, Apollo crews logged one flash about every 2.9 minutes. All but one astronaut saw them.
They're cosmic rays. Charged particles from deep space pass straight through your eye and trigger the retina, like a particle trail in a cloud chamber.
Over the South Atlantic, where radiation is ten to a hundred times stronger, one astronaut counted several flashes a minute as he dozed off.
On the ground, the air above you absorbs them. Go to orbit, close your eyes, and watch the universe hit you in the face.

description:
What if you saw flashes of light with your eyes closed? Apollo astronauts reported exactly that, about one flash every 2.9 minutes in the dark, and ISS astronaut Don Pettit still sees them as he falls asleep.
The flashes are cosmic rays, high-energy charged particles that pass through the retina and trigger it, and they come several times a minute over the South Atlantic Anomaly, where radiation is 10 to 100 times stronger.
